Gandhi. Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, known as Mahatma, or "Great Soul," lived from 1869 to 1948. He was the spiritual and political leader of India's independence movement against British colonial rule.

Born in Gujarat, India, he studied law in England and practiced as a barrister in South Africa. There he developed his philosophy of nonviolent resistance against racist colonial rule.

Through nonviolent civil disobedience and mass mobilization across the Indian subcontinent, he transformed the geography of political resistance and helped secure India's sovereignty in 1947.

He led the Salt March in 1930, a two-hundred-forty-mile journey to the Arabian Sea to protest the British salt monopoly. This sparked mass civil disobedience and imprisoned thousands, including Gandhi himself.

He negotiated India's independence during the twilight of the British Raj, most notably at the Round Table Conferences in London and through correspondence with British leaders.

Gandhi championed the spinning wheel, the charkha, and homespun cloth, khadi, as symbols of Indian self-sufficiency, economic independence, and rejection of British industrial goods.

He advocated for Hindu-Muslim unity and opposed the Partition of India in 1947. He viewed the division into India and Pakistan as a tragic fracture of the subcontinent's political geography.

His assassination came in Delhi in January 1948, when Nathuram Godse, a Hindu extremist opposed to his pluralism and acceptance of Pakistan's creation, killed him.

His philosophy of satyagraha, or truth-force, influenced global movements for justice and decolonization far beyond India's borders. His approach to nonviolent resistance became a model for freedom fighters and civil rights leaders worldwide.
